content.text: The text reviews acute, chronic, tuberculous, cancerous, infantile, and localized peritonitis, emphasizing symptoms such as pain, tenderness, tympanites, absolute constipation, absent peristalsis, vomiting, pallor, fever, scant urine, and diagnostic distinctions from colic and obstruction. It describes historical treatments, especially aggressive opium-induced semi-narcotism, while noting risks in Bright’s disease; it also discusses adhesions, abscesses, perforation, intestinal obstruction, ascites, and hemorrhagic effusions. The author reports visiting hospitals in London, Edinburgh, and Paris, practicing at New York Hospital and Bellevue Hospital, and observing cases in Vermont. Tuberculous peritonitis is generally fatal and treated supportively. The subsequent section defines tabes mesenterica as tuberculosis of mesenteric glands, primarily affecting poorly nourished children, producing abdominal distension, emaciation, anemia, digestive disturbances, fever, and glandular masses; prognosis is grave, with prevention and nutritional palliation emphasized.
